title: Unraveling heterogeneity in endometrial cancer via integrated single cell genotype-phenotype mapping
text:
Endometrial cancer is the most common cancer in the female genital tract but is understudied,
particularly at the single cell level. We aim to leverage our unique biobank of endometrial
cancers with detailed clinical annotations to resolve tumor heterogeneity and clonal evolution at
the genetic and transcriptomic level via novel and innovative technologies. Our findings may
unveil molecular associations of tumor recurrence and response to specific therapies—an
approach that may be broadly applicable to tumors beyond the endometrium.

title: Leveraging in vivo protein tracking to identify novel immune markers associated with obesity driven disease
text:
PROJECT NARRATIVE.
The intestinal epithelium, responsible for transmitting signals from nutrient and toxin intake, plays a piv-
otal role in interorgan communication during the development of obesity. In this grant, we will determine
how obesity impacts intestinal protein secretion, and how adipose tissue immune cells are affected by
these intestine-secreted proteins during the development of obesity. Characterization of these secreted
biomarkers will contribute to the development of targeted therapeutics, advancing medical practices
and enhancing overall health for individuals affected by obesity-related maladies.

title: Elucidating the Interplay Between DDX41 and CUX1 Mutations in Hematopoiesis in Danio Rerio and iPSCs
text:
Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) is amongst the most common hematological malignancies of the elderly, with
limited treatment options and understanding of disease pathogenesis, and may often progress to acute myeloid
leukemia (AML). While germline mutations in the DEAD-box Helicase 41 gene (DDX41) have been identified in
patients with MDS, it is not yet understood what secondary factors or genetic aberrations drive DDX41 germline
patients from quiet to smoldering disease; thus the goal of my proposal is to delineate how DDX41 and a highly
common secondary mutation in CUT-like homeobox 1 (CUX1) cooperate to drive hematopoietic dysfunction.
Understanding the mechanisms behind the disease pathogenesis of hematological malignancies is clinically
important because it can provide novel diagnostic or therapeutic avenues for MDS patients.

title: NAMs-Decisions Center: New Approach Methods for Decisions on Industrial and Consumer-Use Chemicals
text:
The NAMs Decisions Center is a team of scientists and experts working to improve chemical safety testing by
developing modern, non-animal methods (NAMs) that regulators can trust. Their goal is to replace traditional
animal tests with advanced lab models and computer simulations that predict chemical effects more accurately.
By improving how chemicals are compared for safety (a process called read-across), the Center aims to speed
up chemical evaluations, reduce animal testing, and enhance public health protection.

title: RTB 1
text: Pancreatic cancer is a deadly disease with a dismal prognosis and a high frequency of distant metastasis. One likely reason for the frequent metastases in pancreatic cancer is the ability of malignant cells in the primary tumor to invade veins, providing direct access to the liver. While this intravasation is a key first step in metastasis, little is known about the molecular and cellular alterations that underlie this process. Foci of cancer cell intravasation are small and complex, requiring high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) approaches to study them. In this Research Test Bed of our Center for 3D Multiscale Cancer Imaging, we will comprehensively characterize the morphological, cellular, and molecular alterations of foci of intravasation in 3D in human pancreatic cancer samples. In collaboration with Technology Development Unit 1, we will employ our novel deep learning 3D reconstruction approach CODA to serially sectioned pancreatic cancer samples with venous invasion to quantify morphological and cellular features of intravasation. We will also perform multi-dimensional immune profiling of these intravasation foci in 3D using imaging mass cytometry, which can label with 40 antibodies on each tissue section. These analyses will allow us to compare the tumor microenvironment in foci of intravasation to that in other areas of cancer and in uninvolved veins. In collaboration with Technology Development Unit 2, we will analyze the gene expression changes in these intravasation foci by applying a newly developed spatial transcriptomics/proteomics approach (DBit-Seq) to pancreatic cancer samples previously reconstructed by CODA. This approach will provide the first 3D multi-scale models of venous invasion in human pancreatic cancer, providing unprecedented morphological, cellular, and molecular detail of the process of intravasation and initiation of metastasis. In addition, our Research Test Bed will provide a critical opportunity to implement, validate, and iteratively improve the novel approaches from the two Technology Development Centers. We will work closely with these Technology Development Centers in order to evaluate the performance of CODA and DBit-Seq in our human pancreatic tissue samples, allowing validation of the cell type identification and molecular alterations by complementary techniques. The studies in our Research Test Bed will promote significant improvement of the CODA and DBit-Seq imaging platforms while also providing important biological insights into the initiation of metastasis in pancreatic cancer.

title: NICHD PEDIATRIC AND MATERNAL RESOURCE CENTER: BRIDGING PHARMACOLOGY AND THE REAL WORLD - BPCA PTN
text: The mission of the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD) is to lead research and training to understand human development, improve reproductive health, enhance the lives of children and adolescents, and optimize abilities for all. The Obstetric and Pediatric Pharmacology and Therapeutics Branch (OPPTB) supports one of the major missions of the NICHD to enhance maternal, pediatric, and infant pharmacology, therapeutics, and drug development. The branch promotes basic, translational, and clinical research to evaluate and improve the safety and efficacy of multiple types of therapeutics, such as (but not limited to) pharmaceutical drugs, biologics, medical devices, and regenerative tissue constructs. The branch develops and supports comprehensive national efforts to increase the knowledge base for understanding appropriate therapeutic treatment of diseases and conditions during pregnancy, the postpartum period, and lactation, and for children during infancy, childhood, and the transition from adolescence to adulthood. Branch-supported research includes expanding the genomic understanding and phenotypic characterization of drug responses and, are not limited to the following: leveraging advanced multi-omics technologies; novel clinical trial approaches, data science, and artificial intelligence methods; and pharmacometric modeling tools to inform prevention and treatment strategies. One of the major activities of the branch is the implementation and management of the Best Pharmaceuticals for Children Act (BPCA) Clinical Program. The objectives of this program include: 1. Provide support for critical infrastructure including clinical trial expertise, pharmacology expertise, and laboratory and biospecimen research including methods/assay developments in order to enhance maternal, pediatric, and adolescent therapeutics and devices. This infrastructure is called the Pediatric Trials Network (Pediatric Trials Network | PTN) which serves as the program infrastructure to conduct and oversee regulatory rigorous pediatric clinical trials that lead to drug label changes. 2. Oversee the conduct of pediatric pharmacology research and training in the US and internationally to address the global problem delays in pediatric and maternal drug development ecosystem, including therapeutics research and workforce improvements. The funding and conduct of clinical research in pediatrics and maternal health offers many challenges and requires a system/program that is flexible and responsive, and that ideally provides coordinated exposure to expertise in this ecosystem. This contract is to provide a supportive and adjunctive program and resource for regulatory rigorous clinical trials conducted within and outside of the PTN clinical infrastructure of clinical coordination.

title: Characterization of Spinal Pathology in Axial Psoriatic Arthritis
text:
Many Americans experience the debilitating consequences of axial disease resulting from Psoriatic Arthritis. The
goal of this project is to optimize imaging tools that could provide doctors improved evaluation of Psoriatic Arthritis
axial disease and help in making treatment regimens more personalized for their patients.

title: Mechanisms of gene regulation in cancer
text:
p53 is the most frequenUy mutated gene in human cancer and we show that select mutations in p53 drive
cancer growth. Our work will illuminate new ways that mutant p53 regulates gene expression to drive
cancer growth. We hope that these studies will lead to new therapeutic approaches for patients with p53
mutations.

title: Precision Engineering of STING-DC Immunity to Overcome Tumor Immune Evasion
text:
This R35 application aims to harness the stimulator of interferon genes (STING) pathway and dendritic
cell biology to restore and boost immune defense against cancer. We will focus on immune engineering
of the molecular and cellular underpinnings of STING signaling by nanotechnology. Through our bench-
to-clinic and back-to-bench approach, our goal is to identify and overcome existing biological and
technological barriers impeding clinical progress, and ultimately apply these insights to establish a
successful STING-targeted therapy in cancer patients unresponsive to current treatments.

title: Quantitative Imaging Analysis to Identify Chronic Respiratory Disease
text:
Veterans are at higher risk for chronic respiratory diseases (CRDs), including chronic obstructive pulmonary
disease (COPD) and interstitial lung disease, relative to the general population due to deployment-related
and occupational exposures and increased rates of smoking. Although early diagnosis and treatment can
improve outcomes, no screening programs for the early detection of CRDs currently exist – as a result, many
CRDs are detected late, often when symptoms are severe. Unlike for CRDs, screening programs for lung
cancer using low-dose chest computed tomography (CT) scans do exist and changes in the lungs due to
CRDs can be detected on these studies. This project will use specialized computer software to analyze chest
CT scans obtained for lung cancer screening to detect changes in the lungs due to CRDs. These computer
measurements will be used to develop a tool to help identify undiagnosed CRD among Veterans so that they
may receive timely, personalized care.

title: Computational de novo design of macrocyclic type I Signal Peptidase inhibitors
text:
Methods for developing new antibiotics are urgently required to address the growing rise of antibiotic resistance
mechanisms. We propose to leverage our recent advances in computational peptide design and integrate them
with high-throughput chemical synthesis to develop inhibitors of a validated antimicrobial target – the type 1
bacterial signal peptidase. The computational and experimental methods developed in this project will be broadly
applicable to developing superior analogs of naturally-occurring antibiotics and rationally designing new classes
of antibiotics.

title: Abatacept for the treatment of Common Variable Immunodeficiency with Interstitial Lung Disease (ABCVILD)  IND #152820 9/2/20
text:
This project will test the safety and efficacy of abatacept for the treatment of granulomatous
lymphocytic interstitial lung disease (GLILD) in individuals with common variable immune
deficiency (CVID). It will also assess biomarkers of response and seek to define subsets of
patients most appropriate for this therapy.

title: Comparative Mitochondrial Health Assessment Core
text: (Comparative Mitochondrial Health Assessment Core) The maintenance of normal mitochondrial bioenergetics and metabolism is essential for healthy aging. Although bioenergetic metrics have been surveyed in a broad range of aging models, integration of these parameters with mitochondrial quality control mechanisms and mitochondrial genetics, and leverage these measurement to translate aging research programs to potential aging therapeutics, are necessary for a better understanding of healthy aging. We will continue to offer our expertise on the interface between mitophagy, mitochondrial function and inflammation in which we have unique expertise. In addition, we offer the techniques needed to determine the impact of mitochondria-nuclear interactions (which also were pioneered at UAB) and pro-inflammatory signaling through mitochondrial Damage Associated Molecular Patterns (mtDAMPs). Molecular energetics, metabolomics techniques and metabolic therapeutics will be applied to model species of special interest to gerontology scientists. In the Comparative Mitochondrial Health Assessment Core (Mitometabolism Core) both state of the art and established techniques in bioenergetics/metabolism, mitochondrial genetics, mitochondrial dynamics/mitophagy and redox biology will be offered. State of the art experimental design, and protocols for assessing cellular bioenergetics in various live and frozen cells/tissues/organisms of aging models can be achieved. The Mitometabolism Core will provide scientific and technical assistance to measure these parameters of mitochondrial quality control. The mitochondrial nuclear exchange (MNX) mice will be offered to the aging community to allow the contribution of specific mitochondrial DNA sequences to the process of aging to be assessed independent of the nuclear contribution. Additional services will be provided to NIA regular and supported members and pilot grant awardees in determination of mechanisms of interaction of small molecule therapeutics with mitochondrial and glycolytic function. This Core will also evaluate other impact of candidate therapeutics on mitophagy and the release of mtDNA DAMPs, using high throughput, sensitive, versatile, optimized approaches that are well- integrated with the whole Metabolism Core. We will also perform mechanistic studies of mitochondrial bioenergetics, supercomplex integrity, and quality control, as well as their regulation by circadian clock, and track the exosomal transfer of mtDNA and mitochondrial electron transport chain complexes. The Mitometabolism Core will also provide education and training in the measures of mitochondrial health.

title: Educational Program on Translating Neural Medical Devices
text: The project will create a comprehensive educational training program on the best practices for successfully navigating the translational pathway for neural medical devices. Our program will provide (1) virtual ‘sprints’ through a series of freely-available video lectures with topical exercises and round-table discussions and (2) three-day workshops with program faculty that will provide participants with hands-on exercises designed around relevant case studies and participant interests.

title: Radiation and dendritic cell combination to improve immunotherapy response in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma
text:
Patients with unresectable, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma have poor overall survival. We propose to
examine the clinical activities and immune effect of a novel combination therapy using radiation followed by
intratumor injection of autologous dendritic cells followed by systemic infusion of checkpoint inhibitors to PD-L1
and TIGIT.

title: CD40: a gatekeeper of natural antibody production in atherosclerosis
text:
Co-stimulatory immune checkpoints are master regulators of inflammation. We discovered that CD40 on innate
type B-cells (B1 cells) protects against atherosclerosis. We propose to unravel how CD40 maintains B1 cell
homeostasis in atherosclerosis and how B1 cell CD40 levels correlate with coronary artery disease, thereby
unlocking its potential as immunotherapeutic target and biomarker for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

title: Role of human-specific haplotype diversity on cell fate commitment
text:
Genomic diversity is a fundamental aspect of human natural history. Variations in susceptibility to
complex diseases within the human population highlight the significance of understanding
genomic diversity to uncover previously unknown mechanisms of common diseases risk. This
proposal seeks to elucidate the contribution of human-specific genomic diversity to the regulation
of cell fate commitment and the maintenance of cellular states across a spectrum of cell types.

title: Characterizing cancer susceptibility mechanisms for TERT/CLPTM1L and other telomere-related regions
text:
Inherited genetic variation in the TERT gene region influences risk for many types of cancer and many human
traits related to aging and cellular replication, including telomere length, epigenetic aging, blood cell traits, and
somatic mutations. We propose to comprehensively characterize variation in this region across all relevant
traits, examining shared effects, biological mechanisms, and extending our analyses to evaluate the cancer
relevance of other genes/regions known to impact telomere length. The proposed project will increase our
understanding of the critical roles of TERT and telomere length in cancer susceptibility, aging, and human
health, supporting future efforts to leverage telomere biology to develop interventions for the prevention and
treatment of cancer and other aging-related diseases.

title: Micro and Nanofluidic Technologies for Conveying the Central Dogma in Biology and Precision Medicine
text: The National Center for Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering (NCBIB) funded BioModular Multi-Scale Systems (CBM2) for Precision Medicine will develop tools to realize precision medicine by generating multi-omics information to provide better outcomes for patients. The Technology Training and Dissemination (TT&D) theme in Phase III will be “Micro- and Nanofluidic Tools for Conveying the Central Dogma in Biology” and will be synchronized with the technology research and development (TR&D) projects’ outputs. The cornerstone of our TT&D will be the innovations emanating from the TR&Ds and the vast array of CPs and SPs that provide compelling applications of our technologies. CBM2’s TR&D will create infrastructure that addresses challenges related to the molecular analysis of mass-limited samples typically associated with liquid biopsies. The ambitious and innovative goals of the TT&D will be realized through an accomplished team of multi- disciplinary researchers. The Center’s participants will train peers and disseminate knowledge and expertise into a scientific community in several compelling areas: micro- and nanofabrication, plastics engineering, single molecule analyses, molecular biology, surface chemistry, and machine learning. We will emphasize engineering differences between macro/micro/nanoscales, physical property variations as dimensions change, and the effect of surfaces on the chemical and/or biological processes carried out at mixed-scales. TT&D will serve as the public relations arm of CBM2 and will be tasked with training, communicating, and disseminating TR&D scientific and technological advancements to peers, students/post-doctoral fellows (i.e., future emissaries of our technologies) and the general public. There will be innovative activities designed for all groups; these will include hands-on technical workshops dedicated to fabrication and device operation, webinars on biomarkers in clinical testing and validation, big data analysis, machine learning, and rigor in scientific research. Findings and discoveries will be disseminated using our website, social media, webinars, protocol catalogs, and user-initiated one-on-one communications. CBM2 will use existing resources within the Center’s affiliated institutions and those generated in Phase III to inform the biomedical community about our technical capabilities. Dissemination of Center discoveries will be enhanced by compelling publications and patents. CBM2 will train and educate non-center affiliated researchers, collaborators, students, physicians, and industry partners and entrepreneurs through its visiting scholar program to recruit scientists for internships at institutions that use Center-developed technologies to provide invaluable training experiences for participants. We will use our skills in mixed-scale fabrication to demonstrate our capabilities during “How to Make It/How to Use It” workshops and disseminate metrics for unique sample processing capabilities. The Center will deliver tutorials, webinars, and protocols on our website, offer workshops on-site and at national/international meetings to disseminate our efforts. Our TT&D will also inform technologists on how to forge relationships with clinicians.

title: A New Immune Checkpoint Pathway in Human Bladder Cancer
text:
The proposed research is directly relevant to public health and NIH’s mission,
because our program will result in new functional and mechanistic understanding
of a new immune checkpoint pathway in human bladder cancer. This new insight
will directly translate into novel immunotherapies for the treatment of human
bladder cancer.
